To use an analogy, if you think of your hair as a house, then the keratin is a major part of the foundation.

Beautiful Hair, Free from Static

articles.title: Scalp Serum for Hair Loss: What It Does and How to Use It
articles.excerpt: How to use a scalp serum for hair loss: what it can do, serum vs tonic, how to apply it, how often, and how long it takes. Salon educator guide.
articles.html:
The short answer

A scalp serum for hair loss is a leave-in treatment you massage into the scalp, not the lengths. It works by keeping the scalp clean, calm and flake-free, which helps reduce shedding from breakage and gives hair a healthier base to grow from. Use it daily, on a clean scalp, for at least a couple of months before you judge it.

Option Texture and feel Best for
Scalp serum A few drops, lightweight, no rinse Shedding plus a dry, itchy or flaky scalp
Scalp tonic Liquid, cooling, no rinse Oily or buildup-prone scalps that like a fresh, tingly feel
Hair (lengths) serum Oil or silicone based Frizz and shine on the ends, not the scalp

In the salon, "Do scalp serums actually work?" is one of the questions we hear most from clients who see more hair in the shower drain or the brush. The honest answer is that a good scalp serum is a scalp care product, not a miracle. Used correctly, it can make a real difference to how your scalp feels and how much hair you lose to breakage. Used on the ends, used once a week, or used instead of seeing a doctor about sudden hair loss, it will disappoint you. This guide covers what a scalp serum can and cannot do, how it differs from a regular hair serum and a tonic, and exactly how to apply it.

Scalp serum for hair loss: what it can and cannot do

Hair grows from follicles in the scalp, and the scalp is skin. When that skin is flaky, itchy, oily or irritated, people scratch, wash harder, and handle their roots roughly, and fragile hair snaps. A scalp serum targets that environment. The ingredients worth looking for are anti-dandruff actives that keep flakes under control, soothing botanicals that calm itching, and light oils that keep the scalp comfortable without clogging it.

What a cosmetic scalp serum can do:

  • Help keep the scalp clean, calm and free of flakes.
  • Reduce itching, so you scratch and break less hair at the root.
  • Help reduce shedding from breakage when it is part of a gentle routine.
  • Leave the roots feeling lighter and fresher than a heavy oil would.

What it cannot do: a cosmetic serum does not treat medical hair loss. If you are losing hair suddenly, in patches, or after illness, childbirth, a medication change or a period of stress, see a dermatologist first. Hair loss has many causes, and a doctor can tell you which one you are dealing with. A scalp serum can still be part of your routine alongside that advice.

Scalp serums vs hair serums: are they the same thing?

No, and mixing them up is the most common mistake we see. A classic "hair serum" is usually a smoothing product, often silicone or oil based, made to coat the lengths and ends for shine and frizz control. Put that on your scalp and you get greasy roots and buildup, which is the opposite of what a shedding scalp needs.

Scalp serums are formulated for skin. They are lighter, they absorb rather than coat, and they are designed to stay on without rinsing. If a product says "hair serum for scalp" on the label, check the directions: it should tell you to part the hair and apply directly to the scalp, not to smooth it over the lengths.

Hair loss serum vs scalp tonic: which one do you need?

Both are leave-in scalp treatments, and both go on after washing. The difference is mostly texture and how your scalp likes to feel.

The Scalp Recovery Anti Hair-Loss Serum is a no-rinse scalp serum made with piroctone olamine, argan oil and tea tree oil. You use a few drops, which makes it a good fit if your scalp runs dry, itchy or flaky and you want something nourishing that does not weigh hair down.

The Scalp Recovery Anti Hair Loss Tonic (90ml) is a liquid with lactobacillus lysate, piroctone olamine, tea tree oil, eucalyptus, menthol and menthyl nicotinate. It gives a cooling, tingling feel and helps remove buildup and excess oil, so clients with oily or buildup-prone scalps usually prefer it. It is color-safe, pH balanced at 4.5 to 5.5, and free from SLS, parabens, silicones and DMDM hydantoin.

You do not need both on the same day. Pick the one that matches your scalp, and stay with it long enough to see results.

Hair shedding serum: what to expect and how long it takes

Hair grows slowly, and the hair you see falling today started its cycle months ago. That is why any scalp routine needs patience. In our experience, clients notice a calmer, less itchy, less flaky scalp within the first few weeks. Changes in how much hair ends up in the brush take longer, so give a daily routine at least two to three months before you decide whether it is working.

Track it simply. Take a photo of your part line in the same light every two weeks, and pay attention to how much hair collects in the drain after washing. Those two checks tell you more than day-to-day impressions.

Shedding from breakage also depends on what you do to your hair outside the serum. Tight ponytails, rough towel drying, very hot tools and harsh washing all add to the hair you lose. The serum works best when the rest of the routine is gentle.

How to use a scalp serum for hair loss

This is the routine we teach for the Scalp Recovery line. It takes about five minutes on wash days and one minute on the days in between.

  1. Cleanse the scalp. Massage the Scalp Recovery Anti Hair Loss Shampoo (300ml) into a wet scalp for 1 to 2 minutes, then rinse. Repeat if needed. Its formula uses piroctone olamine, tea tree and eucalyptus extracts, and it is free from SLS, parabens and silicones.
  2. Condition. Apply the Scalp Recovery Conditioner to clean, damp hair, leave it on for 2 to 3 minutes, and rinse well.
  3. Towel dry gently. Press the water out instead of rubbing. Wet hair breaks easily.
  4. Part the hair. Make small sections so you can reach the scalp itself, especially along the part line, the crown and any thinning areas.
  5. Apply a few drops of serum directly to the scalp. Not the lengths, not the ends.
  6. Massage for one minute with your fingertips, not your nails. Small circles, light pressure.
  7. Do not rinse. Style as usual.

On non-wash days, the serum can also go on dry hair. Part, apply a few drops, massage, done.

Common mistakes

  • Using too much. A few drops is the direction. More product does not mean faster results, just heavier roots.
  • Applying it to the hair instead of the scalp. The scalp is where it needs to be.
  • Skipping days. The serum is designed for daily use. Consistency matters more than amount.
  • Layering heavy oils on top. If you want shine on the ends, keep oils away from the roots.
  • Scrubbing with nails. Scratching an irritated scalp undoes the calming work.

Building a full scalp recovery routine

A serum on its own helps, but the scalp responds best when every step points the same way. That is why the line is built as shampoo, conditioner and a leave-in step. If you want to start with everything at once, the Scalp Recovery Treatment Trio bundles the shampoo, conditioner and tonic. You can browse the serum and other leave-in options in our hair care serums and scalp treatment collection.

Wash frequency matters too. An oily, flaky scalp usually does better washed more often with a gentle cleanser, not less often. If you are unsure what "gentle" means on an ingredient list, our guide to sulfate-free shampoo and who really needs it walks through it.

Frequently asked questions

Does scalp serum help with hair loss?

A cosmetic scalp serum helps the scalp, and a healthy scalp helps reduce shedding from breakage. It does not treat medical causes of hair loss. If your hair loss is sudden, patchy or getting worse quickly, see a dermatologist.

How often should I use a scalp serum?

Daily. The Scalp Recovery serum is designed for daily use, either after washing or on dry hair on the days in between.

Should I put scalp serum on wet or dry hair?

Either. After washing, towel dry first so the serum is not diluted by dripping water. On non-wash days, apply it to a dry scalp.

Do you rinse out scalp serum?

No. It is a leave-in product. Massage it in for about one minute and leave it on.

Can I use a scalp serum and a hair oil together?

Yes, as long as they go in different places. Serum on the scalp, a small amount of oil on the mid-lengths and ends only.

How long does a scalp serum take to work?

Most people feel a calmer, less flaky scalp within a few weeks. For changes in shedding, use it daily for at least two to three months and track your progress with photos.

This article is for general hair care education and is not medical advice. Speak with a dermatologist about ongoing or sudden hair loss.

By the Evoque Professional education team.

articles.title: Milk Leave-In Conditioner: What It Does, Spray vs Cream, and How to Use It
articles.excerpt: What a milk leave-in conditioner does, spray vs creamy hair milk, who it suits, and a step-by-step routine for dry, color-treated hair.
articles.html:
Quick answer: A milk leave-in conditioner is a no-rinse conditioner made with milk-derived protein, usually hydrolyzed milk protein, that helps dry hair hold moisture and comb out without snapping. Spray versions are light and best for fine to medium hair and daily detangling; creamy "hair milk" lotions are heavier and suit thick, coily or very dry hair. Apply it to damp, towel-dried hair from mid-lengths to ends, comb through, and do not rinse.

Format Best for Weight When to use
Two-phase milk spray Fine, medium, color-treated, tangle-prone hair Light Every wash day, before blow-drying, mid-day refresh
Creamy hair milk lotion Thick, curly, coily or very dry hair Medium to rich Wash days, air-drying, curl definition
Rinse-out milk mask Dry, brittle, heat-styled hair Rich Once or twice a week, before the leave-in

"Milk leave in conditioner" comes up again and again in the searches that bring people to our site, along with "milk leave in conditioner spray" and "hair milk leave in conditioner." The confusion is understandable. Some products are called hair milk, some are milk sprays, some are creamy conditioners that happen to contain milk protein, and the labels rarely explain the difference. This guide sorts it out the way we would in a salon education class: what the ingredient does, which format fits which hair, and how to use it so you actually see a difference.

What is a milk leave-in conditioner?

A milk leave-in conditioner is a conditioner you apply after washing and do not rinse out, built around a milk-derived ingredient. In professional formulas that ingredient is almost always hydrolyzed milk protein. "Hydrolyzed" means the protein has been broken into smaller pieces so it can sit on and around the hair cuticle instead of just sliding off. It is not the same as pouring milk on your hair. Fresh milk spoils, smells, and leaves fat on the scalp. A cosmetic milk protein gives you the useful part without the downsides.

What it does in practice:

  • Helps hair hold moisture. Protein fragments bind water, so dry lengths feel softer and less straw-like for longer after styling.
  • Improves slip and combability. Paired with conditioning agents, it lets a wide-tooth comb glide through wet hair, which means less breakage at the ends.
  • Adds a smoother feel and more shine. A smoother cuticle reflects more light and frizzes less.

It is not a bond builder and it does not rebuild hair from the inside. Think of it as daily conditioning that makes dry, porous hair behave better.

Milk leave in conditioner spray vs. creamy hair milk

This is where most people pick the wrong product for their hair type.

Milk leave-in conditioner spray

Sprays are light. The best ones are two-phase: you will see two layers in the bottle, a watery conditioning layer and a lighter protective layer. Shaking mixes them so every spray delivers both. Sprays are ideal if your hair is fine to medium, gets weighed down easily, tangles after washing, or is color-treated and needs protection before a blow-dryer or flat iron.

Our Milk Therapy Two-Phase Leave-In Conditioner spray is built this way. It contains hydrolyzed milk protein and is formulated with 12 essential amino acids, it helps protect against heat up to 450°F / 230°C, and it sits at a pH of 3.5 to 4.5, which helps keep the cuticle closed and smooth. It is sulfate-free and paraben-free and comes in 100ml, 200ml and 400ml sizes.

Hair milk leave-in conditioner (creamy lotion)

Creamy hair milks are thicker, closer to a light lotion. They suit thick, curly and coily textures that drink product and need more weight to stay defined and soft through the day. On fine hair they usually leave the roots flat and the ends greasy by day two.

Simple rule: if you can see your scalp easily through your hair, or your hair goes limp with most products, choose a spray. If your hair is dense, curly or coily and still feels dry an hour after conditioner, a creamy hair milk or layering a spray under a cream works better.

Who should use a milk leave-in conditioner?

Milk protein leave-ins earn their place in these situations:

  • Color-treated or lightened hair that feels rough and tangles when wet.
  • Hair you heat style two or more times a week.
  • Dry climates, including Southern California summers, where hair loses moisture fast.
  • Long hair with dry ends but a normal scalp.

Who should go easy: if your hair already feels stiff, crunchy or snaps when you stretch a wet strand, you may be using too much protein across your routine. Alternate your milk leave-in with a protein-free conditioner for a couple of weeks and see how your hair responds. Healthy hair should stretch slightly and return; hair that does not stretch at all usually needs more moisture, not more protein.

How to use a milk leave-in conditioner (step by step)

  1. Wash and condition. Use a gentle cleanser such as Milk Therapy Hydrating Shampoo, which is sulfate-free and made for dry and color-treated hair, then your regular conditioner or mask.
  2. Towel-dry gently. Squeeze water out; do not rub. Hair should be damp, not dripping, or the leave-in just runs off.
  3. Shake the bottle well if it is a two-phase spray, until the layers fully mix.
  4. Spray mid-lengths to ends first. Hold the bottle about 6 to 8 inches away. For shoulder-length hair start with 4 to 6 sprays; for long or thick hair, 8 to 12. Keep it off the roots unless your scalp is very dry.
  5. Comb through with a wide-tooth comb, starting at the ends and working up.
  6. Style as usual. Blow-dry, flat iron, or air-dry. Do not rinse.
  7. Refresh on day two or three with one or two sprays on dry ends to cut frizz and bring back shine.

Using too much is the most common mistake. If hair feels coated or looks flat, cut the number of sprays in half before deciding the product is wrong for you.

Milk shampoo and conditioner: building a full milk routine

A leave-in works best when the steps before it are not stripping the hair. A full milk protein routine for dry hair looks like this:

  • Cleanse: a gentle milk protein shampoo, 2 to 3 times a week for dry hair. We explain how milk protein works in a cleanser, and how to avoid protein overload, in our guide to milk protein shampoo for dry hair.
  • Condition: a matching hydrating conditioner on mid-lengths and ends, 2 to 3 minutes.
  • Treat: a rinse-out mask once or twice a week in place of conditioner.
  • Protect: the leave-in spray every wash day.

If you want the three daily steps together, the Milk Therapy Power Trio (shampoo, conditioner and two-phase leave-in) bundles the 1L shampoo, 1L conditioner and 400ml leave-in for $89. You can see every size and format in the Evoque Milk Therapy collection.

Milk hair mask or milk leave-in: do you need both?

They do different jobs. A mask is a rinse-out treatment with a higher concentration of conditioning ingredients; you leave it on for several minutes and wash it off. A leave-in stays on the hair all day to manage tangles, frizz and heat.

If your hair is mildly dry, the leave-in alone is usually enough. If it is brittle, heavily lightened or heat styled often, add a mask once or twice a week. The Milk Therapy Deep Treatment Masque is applied after shampooing, left on for 5 to 10 minutes and rinsed. It is not a leave-in, so follow it with the spray.

Common mistakes with leave-in milk conditioner

  • Applying to soaking wet hair. Water dilutes it and it drips away. Towel-dry first.
  • Starting at the roots. Roots rarely need it and will look flat. Start at the ends.
  • Skipping the shake on a two-phase formula. You only get half the product.
  • Stacking several protein products every day. If hair turns stiff, rotate in protein-free moisture.
  • Treating it as your only heat protection on very high heat. Check the temperature rating and keep tools at or below it.

FAQ

What does a milk leave-in conditioner do for hair?

It helps dry hair hold moisture, makes wet hair easier to comb, reduces frizz and adds shine. Formulas with heat protection also help shield hair during blow-drying and flat ironing.

Is a milk leave-in conditioner spray good for fine hair?

Yes, a spray is usually the best choice for fine hair because it is light. Use fewer sprays, focus on the ends, and avoid creamy hair milks, which tend to weigh fine hair down.

What is the difference between hair milk and a leave-in conditioner?

"Hair milk" usually refers to a creamy, lotion-like leave-in, often for curly or coily hair. A milk leave-in conditioner can be a cream or a light spray. Both stay in the hair; the difference is texture and weight.

Can I use a milk leave-in conditioner every day?

Yes. A light spray can be used every wash day and as a refresher on dry ends between washes. If hair starts to feel stiff, use it less often or alternate with a protein-free product.

Should I use milk shampoo and conditioner with a milk leave-in?

It is not required, but it helps. A sulfate-free milk shampoo and a hydrating conditioner prepare the hair so the leave-in has less work to do and results last longer between washes.

Is a milk leave-in conditioner safe for color-treated hair?

Most professional milk leave-ins are made for color-treated hair. Our two-phase spray is sulfate-free, paraben-free and made for dry, brittle and color-treated hair.

By the Evoque Professional education team.

articles.title: Leave-In Conditioner and Heat Protectant: Which Goes First?
articles.excerpt: Can you use leave-in conditioner and heat protectant together? Yes. Learn which goes first, when one product is enough, and what is safe for keratin hair.
articles.html:
The short answer

Yes, you can use leave-in conditioner and heat protectant spray together. Apply the leave-in first on towel-dried hair, comb it through, then mist the heat protectant last, right before the blow-dryer or flat iron. If your leave-in is labeled as heat protective, it can do both jobs in one step, so you do not need a second spray.

Your routine What to use
Air-dry, no hot tools Leave-in conditioner only
Blow-dry most days A heat-protective leave-in, one step
Flat iron or curling iron Leave-in first, then a heat protectant rated for your iron temperature
Keratin-treated or color-treated hair A lightweight, heat-protective leave-in made for treated hair

In the salon, the question we hear most at the styling chair is not "which product is best" but "what goes on first." Clients buy a leave-in and a heat protectant, then stand at the mirror with both bottles and no idea how to layer them. This guide answers that, plus the related questions people actually search for: whether a leave-in can replace heat protectant, whether you need both, and what is safe for keratin-treated hair.

Heat protectant spray and leave-in conditioner: what each one does

A leave-in conditioner is a conditioner you do not rinse out. Its job is to detangle, soften, smooth the cuticle and keep moisture in the hair between washes. Most leave-ins are light sprays or creams that you work through the mid-lengths and ends.

A heat protectant is a styling product designed to sit on the surface of the hair and reduce the damage caused by blow-dryers, flat irons and curling irons. Heat protectants usually rely on film-forming ingredients, often silicones such as cyclopentasiloxane or amodimethicone, that coat the strand and help slow down moisture loss when heat hits the hair.

The overlap is bigger than most people think. Many modern leave-in sprays contain the same film-forming ingredients as heat protectants, which is why some of them are formulated and labeled to do both jobs. The label is what matters: if the product does not say it protects against heat, treat it as a conditioner only.

Leave-in conditioner and heat protectant spray: which goes first?

Leave-in conditioner goes first. Heat protectant goes last, right before heat. Here is why that order works:

  • The leave-in needs contact with the hair. It is there to condition the strand, so it should go on clean, towel-dried hair where it can spread evenly.
  • The heat protectant needs to be the outer layer. Its film is what meets the hot air or the iron plates, so it should be the last thing you apply before styling.
  • Comb between the two. Combing the leave-in through first means the heat protectant lands on detangled hair and coats it evenly instead of sitting on knots.

If you use a hair oil or serum, it usually goes after heat styling as a finisher, unless the serum itself is labeled as heat protective. In that case a few drops on damp ends before blow-drying is fine.

Can a leave-in conditioner be used as a heat protectant?

Only if it says so on the label. Some leave-ins are formulated with heat protection, and some are not. A plain leave-in conditioner will still make hair softer and easier to brush, which reduces breakage from pulling, but it is not designed to stand up to direct heat from an iron.

Several leave-ins in the Evoque Professional line are made to do both jobs:

  • The Smart Keratin Leave-In Conditioner Spray is a lightweight mist with keratin-based amino acids, argan oil and macadamia oil. It provides UV and thermal heat protection up to 450°F / 230°C, detangles, and controls frizz and flyaways. It comes in a 400ml size and a 100ml travel size.
  • The Miracle Touch Leave-In Conditioner is an ultra-lightweight prep spray for all hair types. It forms a protective water shield that blocks humidity, guards against heat damage from styling tools, works as a bond-builder and reduces blow-dry time. It comes in 150ml.
  • The Healthy Care Reconstructive Two-Phase Leave-In Conditioner is a two-phase spray with hydrolyzed keratin and argan extract, made for color-treated, normal or dry hair. It helps protect color from fading and helps shield hair from UV and heat. It comes in 400ml.

With any of these, you can skip a separate heat protectant for everyday blow-drying. If you flat iron at high settings, check that the temperature on your iron stays within what your product is rated for. The Smart Keratin Leave-In is the one in this group with a stated temperature rating, which is why it is our pick for flat-iron days.

Do you need both a leave-in and a heat protectant?

It depends on how you style.

You probably need only one product if you blow-dry a few times a week and your leave-in is labeled heat protective. Layering two film-forming sprays on top of each other can make fine hair feel coated and limp, so one good product is often better than two.

You may want both if you have thick, coarse or very dry hair that needs more conditioning than a light spray gives, and you use a flat iron or curling iron regularly. In that case use a richer leave-in first for moisture, then a heat protectant as the top layer.

You need neither for heat if you air-dry. A leave-in alone is enough for softness, detangling and frizz control.

Leave-in conditioner safe for keratin treated hair

After a keratin or smoothing treatment, the goal is to keep the hair smooth for as long as possible. That means a gentle shampoo, no harsh clarifying products, and a leave-in that adds slip without stripping or weighing the hair down.

The Smart Keratin Leave-In Conditioner is made specifically for this. It is designed to help extend and protect keratin and smoothing treatments, it is sulfate-free and paraben-free, and because it also protects against heat, it fits the blow-dry routine most people use to keep a keratin finish sleek. Spray it on damp or dry hair, focus on mid-lengths and ends, comb through and style.

For a full aftercare plan, including how long to wait before washing and which shampoo to use, read our guide on how to make a keratin treatment last longer.

Heat protectant leave-in conditioner vs serum

Sprays and serums can both protect against heat, but they feel different on the hair:

  • Sprays are lighter and spread evenly over the whole head. They suit fine and normal hair and anyone who does not want residue.
  • Serums and oils are more concentrated. They suit thick, dry, frizz-prone ends and give more shine. The Smart Keratin Oil Serum contains keratin-based amino acids, argan oil and macadamia oil, provides heat and UV protection, and can be used before heat styling to protect and after styling for extra shine and frizz control.

A combination many of our stylists use on thick hair: leave-in spray all over, a few drops of serum on the ends only, then blow-dry.

How to use leave-in conditioner and heat protectant: a simple routine

  1. Wash and condition. Rinse well, then gently squeeze water out with a towel. Do not rub.
  2. Apply the leave-in. Shake the bottle, then spray evenly from mid-lengths to ends. Use less near the roots if your hair is fine.
  3. Comb through. Use a wide-tooth comb, working up from the ends.
  4. Wait a few minutes. The Miracle Touch Leave-In directions call for 5 minutes before blow-drying so the formula can absorb. This is a good habit with any leave-in.
  5. Add heat protection if needed. If your leave-in is not heat protective, or you are about to use a flat iron, mist a heat protectant now as the final layer.
  6. Style. Blow-dry with the nozzle pointed down the hair shaft, then use hot tools on fully dry hair only.
  7. Finish. Smooth a drop of serum over the ends if you want extra shine.

Want more detail on amounts and hair-type tips? See our guide on how to use leave-in conditioner the right way, or browse the full leave-in conditioner collection.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using a flat iron on damp hair. Hot tools should only touch fully dry hair, whatever products you use.
  • Spraying the roots heavily. This is the fastest way to make hair look flat and oily by the afternoon.
  • Assuming every leave-in protects from heat. Read the label. If heat protection is not listed, add a heat protectant.
  • Stacking too many products. If your hair feels coated, drop one product. A single heat-protective leave-in is often enough.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use leave-in conditioner and heat protectant together?

Yes. Apply the leave-in first on towel-dried hair, comb it through, then apply the heat protectant as the last step before heat styling.

Does heat protectant go before or after leave-in conditioner?

After. The heat protectant should be the outer layer, so it goes on last, right before the blow-dryer or iron.

Can keratin be a leave-in conditioner?

Keratin itself is a protein, not a product, but many leave-in conditioners contain hydrolyzed keratin or keratin-based amino acids. The Smart Keratin Leave-In Conditioner and the Healthy Care Reconstructive Two-Phase Leave-In both contain hydrolyzed keratin and are used without rinsing.

Is leave-in conditioner safe for keratin treated hair?

Yes, as long as it is gentle and lightweight. The Smart Keratin Leave-In Conditioner is made to help extend and protect keratin and smoothing treatments, and it is sulfate-free and paraben-free.

Do I still need heat protectant if my leave-in says it protects from heat?

For everyday blow-drying, usually not. If you use a flat iron at a high setting, make sure your product is rated for that temperature, or add a dedicated heat protectant as the last layer.

How do I apply leave-in conditioner before blow-drying?

Spray it evenly on towel-dried hair from mid-lengths to ends, comb it through, wait a few minutes so it can absorb, then blow-dry.

By the Evoque Professional education team.

articles.title: Milk Protein Shampoo: What It Does for Dry Hair and How to Choose One
articles.excerpt: What milk protein does for dry, brittle and color-treated hair, how to avoid protein overload, and how to pick the right milk protein shampoo.
articles.html:
The short answer

A milk protein shampoo uses hydrolyzed milk protein, broken down into small pieces, to help dry hair hold moisture and feel smoother and more elastic after washing. It works best for dry, brittle, dull or color-treated hair. For most people the right setup is a gentle, sulfate-free milk protein shampoo, a moisturizing conditioner, and a protein mask no more than once or twice a week.

Your hair Good fit for milk protein?
Dry, rough, dull Yes, this is the main use
Color-treated or bleached Yes, choose a sulfate-free formula
Brittle, snaps easily Yes, balance it with moisture
Already stiff or straw-like after protein products Pause protein and focus on moisture

What is milk protein in shampoo?

Milk naturally contains two main groups of protein, casein and whey. In hair care these are hydrolyzed, which means they are broken into much smaller pieces. On the ingredient list you will usually see it as Hydrolyzed Milk Protein.

Small protein fragments can attach to the surface of the hair, especially where the cuticle is rough or damaged. That is why milk protein formulas tend to leave dry hair feeling softer, smoother and less fragile. In a well-made shampoo, milk protein is usually paired with humectants and amino acids that help pull water into the hair and keep it there.

What does milk protein do for dry hair?

  • Helps hold moisture. Protein and amino acids help dry strands retain water after washing instead of feeling rough as soon as they dry.
  • Smooths the surface. By settling into rough spots on the cuticle, milk protein helps hair feel smoother and reflect more light, so it looks shinier.
  • Improves elasticity. Hair that stretches a little before it breaks is less likely to snap when you brush or style it.
  • Makes washing gentler. In a sulfate-free base, milk protein helps the shampoo cleanse without leaving dry hair squeaky and stripped.

Is milk protein good for color-treated hair?

Yes, with one condition: the shampoo itself should be gentle. Color and bleach roughen the cuticle, which is exactly where milk protein helps most. Pair it with a sulfate-free cleansing base so the shampoo is not stripping the hair while the protein is trying to smooth it. For more on what "sulfate-free" really means, see our guide to sulfate-free shampoo.

Can you use too much protein? Avoiding protein overload

You can. If you stack several protein-heavy products every wash, some hair types, especially fine or low-porosity hair, can start to feel stiff, straw-like or more brittle. That is usually called protein overload.

The fix is balance, not avoidance:

  • Use a milk protein shampoo as your everyday cleanser, then follow with a moisturizing conditioner.
  • Keep intensive protein masks to once or twice a week.
  • If hair starts to feel stiff, skip the mask for a week and use only conditioner and a light leave-in.

Milk protein vs keratin: which one do you need?

Both are proteins, but they suit different goals. Milk protein formulas are usually built around softness and moisture for dry, brittle hair. Keratin formulas are usually built around smoothing frizz and strengthening hair that has been chemically treated or heat styled, and around making a salon keratin treatment last longer. If your main problem is dryness, start with milk protein. If your main problem is frizz or you have had a keratin treatment, start with keratin. Our keratin aftercare guide covers that routine.

How to choose a milk protein shampoo

  1. Check that milk protein is actually there. Look for "Hydrolyzed Milk Protein" on the ingredient list, not just a milky name or scent.
  2. Look for moisture partners. Amino acids, sodium PCA, sodium lactate and glycerin help the protein do its job on dry hair.
  3. Prefer a sulfate-free base if your hair is dry, colored or bleached.
  4. Buy it as a system. A matching conditioner and leave-in make the biggest difference for very dry hair.
  5. Pick the right size. Try a travel size first, then move to a salon size once you know it works for you.

A simple milk protein routine for dry hair

  1. Wash: massage Milk Therapy Hydrating Shampoo into wet hair and scalp, then rinse. It combines hydrolyzed milk protein, amino acids and immortelle extract in a sulfate-free formula.
  2. Condition: apply Milk Therapy Hydrating Conditioner to damp hair, leave it for 1 to 2 minutes and rinse.
  3. Once or twice a week: swap the conditioner for the Milk Therapy Deep Treatment Masque and leave it on for 5 to 10 minutes.
  4. Before styling: spray the Milk Therapy Two-Phase Leave-In on damp hair from mid-lengths to ends. It detangles and helps protect from heat up to 450°F / 230°C.

You can see the whole line in the Milk Therapy collection.

Frequently asked questions

What does milk protein do for hair?

Hydrolyzed milk protein helps dry hair hold moisture and feel smoother, softer and more elastic. It works best paired with amino acids and humectants.

Is milk protein shampoo good for dry hair?

Yes. Dry, brittle and dull hair is exactly what milk protein shampoos are designed for, especially in a gentle, sulfate-free base.

Can I use a milk protein shampoo every day?

A gentle milk protein shampoo can be used on every wash day. Very dry hair usually does not need daily washing, so every second or third day is often enough.

Does milk protein cause protein overload?

It can if you layer many protein products every wash. Use a moisturizing conditioner every time and keep protein masks to once or twice a week.

Is milk protein shampoo safe for color-treated hair?

Yes, if the formula is sulfate-free. Milk protein helps smooth the rough cuticle that coloring and bleaching leave behind.

Milk protein or keratin for frizz?

For frizz and keratin treatment aftercare, keratin is usually the better first choice. For dryness and brittleness, start with milk protein.

By the Evoque Professional education team.

articles.title: Purple Mousse for Blonde Hair: How to Use It and Choose the Best One
articles.excerpt: Learn how to use purple mousse on blonde, bleached and silver hair, how it differs from purple shampoo, and how to choose the best one for your shade.
articles.html:
Quick answer

Purple mousse is a toning foam for blonde hair: violet pigment cancels yellow and brassy tones while you style. Apply a small amount to clean, towel-dried hair, comb it through from mid-lengths to ends, and style as usual. Use it between purple shampoo washes to keep blonde, platinum, silver and white hair cool-toned every day, not just on wash day.

Product Rinse or leave in? Best for
Purple mousse (tone and style) Leave in Daily toning plus body and frizz control
Purple toning foam (rinse-out) Rinse after 3 to 5 minutes A stronger weekly tone boost
Purple shampoo Rinse after 2 to 5 minutes Cleansing and toning on wash day
Purple mask Rinse after 1 to 2 minutes Toning plus softness for dry lengths

Most blondes know purple shampoo. Fewer know what to do on the days they do not wash. That is where purple mousse comes in. It puts a light layer of violet pigment on the hair and leaves it there, so brassiness gets corrected while you style instead of only in the shower. Below, our education team explains how purple mousse works, how to use it without staining or crunch, and how to choose the best purple mousse for your shade.

What is purple mousse for hair?

Purple mousse is a foam styler that carries violet pigment. Violet sits opposite yellow on the color wheel, so a thin veil of it neutralizes the warm, yellow cast that shows up in lightened hair after sun, hard water, heat styling and time. The foam texture is the point: it spreads evenly through the hair with less product than a cream, it adds lift at the root, and it does not have to be rinsed.

Think of it as maintenance between services. It will not lift or change your base color. It keeps the tone your colorist created looking fresh for longer, and it covers you on days when you are not washing.

Purple mousse for blonde hair: who it works best for

Purple mousse is made for light hair, because pigment only shows where there is little natural color underneath. It suits:

  • Bleached and highlighted blonde that turns yellow within a week or two of toning.
  • Platinum and icy blonde, where even a small amount of warmth is visible.
  • Silver, grey and white hair, which can pick up a yellow cast from minerals and styling heat.
  • Naturally light blonde that looks dull or slightly brassy.

If your blonde leans orange rather than yellow (common on darker bases lifted to level 7 or 8), violet will soften it but blue-based toners correct orange more effectively. Ask your colorist which family your hair needs.

Our Flawless Blonde Purple Mousse is designed for both bleached and naturally light hair, including blonde, highlighted, platinum, silver and white. It tones and styles in one step: violet pigment cancels yellow and brassy tones while the lightweight foam adds body and bounce. It also contains 12 amino acids to help revitalize lightened hair and add shine, plus Argan Oil and Keratin Oil for a softer, smoother, anti-frizz finish.

How to use purple mousse on blonde hair

Always follow the directions on your bottle first. For a leave-in, tone-and-style mousse, this is the routine we teach in the salon:

  1. Start with clean, towel-dried hair. Damp hair takes pigment more evenly than soaking wet hair, and more gently than dry hair.
  2. Shake the can, then dispense a golf-ball-sized amount into your palm. Fine or shoulder-length hair needs less; long or thick hair may need two portions.
  3. Work from mid-lengths to ends first. Lightened ends are the most porous and the most brassy. Then use what is left on your hands at the root for lift.
  4. Comb through with a wide-tooth comb so no section gets a heavier dose than the rest. Uneven application is the main cause of patchy lilac spots.
  5. Blow-dry or air-dry as you normally would. Lifting the root with a round brush gives the most volume.
  6. Wash your hands straight away so pigment does not transfer to towels or skin.

Do a strand test the first time. Very porous, freshly bleached or white hair can grab violet pigment fast. Try the mousse on a hidden section underneath before using it all over.

Purple mousse vs purple shampoo: do you need both?

They do different jobs, and most blondes get the best result from using them together.

  • Purple shampoo cleanses and tones in one step on wash day. Our Purple Shampoo for Blonde, Silver and Platinum Hair is left on for 2 to 3 minutes for subtle toning, or up to 5 minutes for stronger correction. Its formula contains sodium lauryl sulfate, so it is not a sulfate-free shampoo; most blondes use it as a toning step rather than at every wash.
  • Purple mousse stays on the hair. It keeps working on non-wash days and adds styling benefits, so you can wash less often without the yellow creeping back.

If you are not sure how often to use purple shampoo for your shade, read our guide on how often to use purple shampoo on blonde and bleached hair. A good rule: once you add a toning mousse, many blondes can cut purple shampoo back by one wash a week.

Rinse-out purple foam vs leave-in purple mousse

Not every purple foam is a styler. Some are rinse-out treatments, and mixing them up is a common mistake.

The Flawless Blonde Purple Toning Foam is a rinse-out toner. Apply it to wet hair after shampooing, leave it on for 3 to 5 minutes depending on how brassy your hair is, then rinse thoroughly with warm water. Use it 1 to 2 times a week. It is also enriched with 12 essential amino acids. Choose it when you want a stronger toning boost than a shampoo gives, without leaving pigment on the hair afterwards.

Choose the leave-in Purple Mousse when you want daily, gentle toning plus volume and frizz control. Many clients use the rinse-out foam once a week and the mousse on styling days.

Best purple mousse for blonde hair: what to look for

When you compare purple mousses, ignore the hype and check five things:

  1. Leave-in or rinse-out. Read the directions. A leave-in mousse should say to style after applying; a rinse-out foam will give a timing and tell you to rinse.
  2. Pigment strength. Platinum and white hair need gentler, buildable pigment. Brassier, darker blondes can handle more.
  3. Care ingredients. Lightened hair is porous and fragile. Look for amino acids, lightweight oils and anti-frizz conditioners rather than a pure styling formula.
  4. Hold and feel. You want body and movement, not crunch. A soft, flexible finish is easier to brush out and re-style the next day.
  5. Who it is made for. Some mousses are tested on silver and white hair, others only on blonde. If you are grey or white, pick one that names your shade.

How to use it: a simple weekly routine

  • Wash day 1: Purple Shampoo, 2 to 3 minutes. Follow with the Purple Mask for Blonde, Silver and Platinum Hair on mid-lengths and ends for 1 to 2 minutes, then rinse. Towel-dry and style with Purple Mousse.
  • Wash day 2: Your regular gentle shampoo and conditioner, then Purple Mousse to style.
  • Once a week if brass shows: swap in the Purple Toning Foam after shampoo, 3 to 5 minutes, then rinse.
  • Every styling day: use heat protection and keep hot tools at moderate settings. Heat is one of the fastest ways to turn blonde warm.

You can browse the full lineup in our Flawless Blonde purple hair care collection.

Frequently asked questions

Is purple mousse good for blonde hair?

Yes. Purple mousse is one of the easiest ways to keep blonde hair cool between salon toning appointments, because it tones on days you do not wash. It works best on light blonde, platinum, silver and white hair.

Can you use purple mousse on bleached hair?

Yes, and bleached hair often benefits most, since it turns yellow quickly. Because bleached hair is porous, start with a small amount, apply evenly and strand-test the first time to avoid a lilac tint.

How often should you use purple mousse?

A leave-in toning mousse can be used every time you style. If you notice a violet cast building up, use it every other styling day or wash with a regular shampoo in between. Rinse-out purple foams are typically used 1 to 2 times a week.

Does purple mousse stain hair or skin?

It can leave a light lilac cast on very porous or white hair if too much is used or it is applied unevenly. Use a small amount, comb it through and wash your hands after applying. A regular shampoo usually lifts any excess.

What is the mousse in the purple bottle?

Many people searching for a "purple bottle mousse" are looking for a purple toning mousse. Our Flawless Blonde Purple Mousse comes in a purple canister and tones and styles blonde, silver and white hair in one step.

Can I use purple mousse instead of purple shampoo?

For light maintenance, sometimes. But mousse does not cleanse, and its pigment dose is lighter. Most blondes keep purple shampoo once or twice a week and use mousse to extend the result.

articles.title: How to Use Leave-In Conditioner the Right Way (And Actually See Results)
articles.excerpt: Learn how to apply leave-in conditioner the right way for soft, detangled, frizz-free hair. Step-by-step guide with expert tips from Evoque USA.
articles.html:
Quick answer: apply leave-in conditioner to clean, damp hair, from mid-lengths to ends, using a small amount (a few sprays or a coin-sized dab). Skip the roots. Most hair types do well with it 2 to 4 times a week, and lightweight sprays can be used daily. Can keratin be a leave-in conditioner? Yes, if the product is a leave-in formula that contains hydrolyzed keratin, such as a keratin leave-in spray. A salon keratin treatment is a different service and cannot be used as a leave-in.

Your hair Leave-in type
Fine or oily Lightweight water-based spray
Frizzy, keratin-treated Keratin leave-in spray or frizz control
Dry, thick, curly Richer leave-in treatment
Color-treated Protein-rich reconstructive leave-in

Updated October 2026 by the Evoque Professional education team.

Why Leave-In Conditioner Deserves a Spot in Your Daily Routine

If you're still skipping leave-in conditioner, your hair is missing out on one of the most hardworking products in hair care. Unlike rinse-out conditioners, leave-ins stay on your strands all day, continuously delivering moisture, smoothing the cuticle, and protecting against heat and environmental damage.

The catch? Most people either use too much, apply it to the wrong hair type, or put it on at the wrong time. This guide walks you through exactly how to do it right.

Who Actually Needs Leave-In Conditioner?

Leave-in conditioner works for almost everyone, but it's especially beneficial if your hair is:

  • Dry or damaged from color, heat, or chemical treatments
  • Prone to frizz or flyaways
  • Thick, curly, or coily
  • Tangly and difficult to comb through
  • Exposed to daily heat styling

Even fine hair can benefit. You just need to apply it more sparingly and focus on the mid-lengths and ends, not the roots.

Step-by-Step: How to Apply Leave-In Conditioner Correctly

Step 1: Start with freshly washed, towel-dried hair

Leave-in conditioner works best on clean, damp hair. After washing, gently squeeze out excess water with a microfiber towel. Avoid rough towel-drying, which raises the cuticle and causes frizz. Your hair should be damp but not dripping.

Step 2: Section your hair (especially if it's thick)

Working in sections ensures every strand gets even coverage. For short or fine hair, you can skip this step and apply all at once.

Step 3: Spray or apply evenly from mid-length to ends

This is the most important step: avoid the roots. Applying leave-in to your roots can weigh hair down and make it look greasy. Focus on the mid-lengths and ends, the areas most prone to dryness and breakage.

For a two-phase spray formula like the Milk Therapy Two Phase Leave-In Conditioner, shake the bottle first to combine the water and oil phases, then spray evenly through damp hair. It's lightweight enough to use daily without buildup.

Step 4: Comb through gently

Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to distribute the product and work through any tangles. Start from the ends and work your way up toward the roots to minimize breakage.

Step 5: Style as usual

You can blow-dry, air-dry, diffuse, or straighten your hair after applying leave-in. The conditioner creates a protective layer that helps shield strands from heat damage.

Can Keratin Be a Leave-In Conditioner?

It depends on what you mean by keratin, because the word covers two very different things.

Keratin in a product. Many conditioners and leave-ins contain hydrolyzed keratin, a protein broken into small pieces so it can sit on and in the hair fiber. In a leave-in formula this helps smooth, strengthen and reduce frizz on damaged or chemically treated hair. Yes, this works as a leave-in. The Smart Keratin Leave-In Conditioner is a lightweight spray made with keratin-based amino acids, argan oil and macadamia oil. You spray it on damp or dry hair, comb through and do not rinse. The Smart Keratin Frizz Control Leave-In works the same way and is aimed at humidity and flyaways. Both list heat protection up to 450°F (230°C).

A keratin treatment. A salon keratin smoothing treatment is a professional service that is applied, dried and sealed with heat. It is not a leave-in, and you should never leave a treatment product in your hair at home. What a leave-in can do is help the result last. After a treatment, a keratin leave-in is a good daily step. Our guide on how to make a keratin treatment last longer covers the full aftercare routine.

One caution: protein is useful, but more is not always better. If your hair starts to feel stiff or straw-like, you are likely overdoing protein. Switch to a moisturizing leave-in for a week or two.

Common Leave-In Conditioner Mistakes to Avoid

  • Using too much: A little goes a long way. Start with a small amount; you can always add more, but you can't take it away.
  • Applying to dry hair: Leave-in conditioner is most effective on damp hair because it seals in the moisture your hair already has. Keratin spray leave-ins are an exception and can also be used on dry hair for a quick smoothing touch-up.
  • Skipping it after color treatments: Colored hair is especially porous and needs extra moisture. Leave-in is non-negotiable post-color.
  • Using a heavy formula on fine hair: Choose a lightweight spray formula if your hair is thin or gets oily quickly.

How Often Should You Use Leave-In Conditioner?

For most hair types, every wash day is ideal, meaning 2 to 4 times per week. If your hair is very dry or heavily damaged, you can use a lightweight spray formula daily between wash days to refresh and re-moisturize.

The Right Leave-In for Your Hair Type

Not all leave-in conditioners are created equal. Here's a quick guide:

  • Fine or oily hair: Choose a lightweight, water-based spray like the Milk Therapy Two Phase Leave-In Conditioner. It absorbs fast and won't weigh hair down.
  • Dry, flat hair that needs volume: the Milk Therapy Mousse, a weightless volumizing mousse with milk proteins, applied to damp hair before blow-drying.
  • Dry, thick, or curly hair: a richer leave-in treatment such as the Yogurt Leave-In Deep Treatment Mask.
  • Frizz and humidity: the Miracle Touch Leave-In Conditioner or the Smart Keratin Frizz Control if your hair is keratin-treated.
  • Color-treated or chemically processed hair: Prioritize a formula with protein and bond-strengthening ingredients, like the Reconstructive Leave-In Conditioner.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can keratin be a leave-in conditioner?

Yes, when it is a leave-in formula containing hydrolyzed keratin, such as a keratin leave-in spray. A salon keratin treatment is a separate service and should not be used as a leave-in.

Can I use leave-in conditioner every day?

Lightweight spray leave-ins are designed for daily use. Richer creams and masks are better 2 to 4 times a week, or the hair can feel heavy.

Should leave-in conditioner go on wet or dry hair?

Damp hair is best, because the product seals in the water already in the hair. A light mist on dry hair is fine as a mid-day refresh with a spray formula.

Do I rinse out leave-in conditioner?

No. That is the point of a leave-in. If you used a rinse-out conditioner or a mask first, rinse that, then apply the leave-in.

Does leave-in conditioner help after a keratin treatment?

Yes. It adds moisture and smoothness between washes and helps keep frizz down. Pair it with a sulfate-free shampoo for the best aftercare; see our sulfate-free shampoo guide to check what the label really means.

Final Thoughts

Leave-in conditioner is one of the simplest ways to upgrade your hair health over time. Apply it consistently on damp hair, avoid the roots, and choose a formula suited to your hair type, and you'll notice softer, smoother, more manageable hair within just a few weeks.

Ready to try it? Explore the Evoque Milk Therapy collection, a milk protein shampoo, conditioner and leave-in conditioner range for dry and color-treated hair, or browse all leave-in conditioners.

By the Evoque Professional education team.

"Sulfate-free" has been printed on shampoo bottles for long enough that most people assume it matters without knowing why. Some of the claims made about sulfates are overstated. Some are entirely accurate. It is worth knowing which is which before you spend more on a bottle.

What sulfates are

Sulfates are surfactants, cleansing agents that let water lift oil and dirt off a surface. The two you will see most often are sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) and sodium laureth sulfate (SLES). They are cheap, extremely effective, and responsible for the thick lather people associate with hair feeling clean.

That effectiveness is the whole problem. Sulfates do not distinguish between the oil you want gone and the lipids, proteins and color pigment you want to keep.

What sulfates are not

To be fair to them: sulfates are not carcinogenic, they do not cause hair loss, and there is no credible evidence linking them to serious health harm at the concentrations used in shampoo. Much of the alarm around them online is marketing rather than science.

The real case against sulfates is narrower and more practical: they are too aggressive for hair that has been chemically processed, and they irritate sensitive scalps.

Who genuinely benefits from switching

Color-treated hair

This is the clearest case. Sulfates open the cuticle and flush dye molecules out with each wash. If you color your hair, sulfate shampoo is one of the biggest reasons your color fades before your next appointment. Reds, coppers and fashion shades fade fastest.

Switching to a color-safe, sulfate-free shampoo such as Milk Therapy is the highest-return change most people with dyed hair can make.

Keratin and chemically-straightened hair

Sulfates strip the keratin out of a treatment. A three-to-five month treatment can be reduced to six weeks by continuing with a sulfate shampoo. If you have paid for a keratin service, sulfate-free is not optional.

Dry, damaged and high-porosity hair

Damaged hair has a raised, porous cuticle and cannot hold moisture well to begin with. Sulfates remove the natural oils that partially compensate. If your hair feels like straw after washing, the shampoo is a likely cause.

Curly and coily hair

Curl patterns make it difficult for scalp oil to travel down the hair shaft, so the ends are naturally drier. Removing what little oil reaches them makes frizz and breakage worse.

Sensitive or eczema-prone scalps

SLS in particular is a known skin irritant and is used as a standard positive control in dermatological patch testing. If your scalp is itchy, tight or flaky, this is worth ruling out.

Blonde and bleached hair

Bleached hair is porous by definition. It loses moisture and toner fast, and sulfates accelerate both.

Who probably doesn't need to bother

If your hair is virgin (never colored, never chemically treated), naturally oily, and your scalp is comfortable, sulfates are unlikely to cause you problems. Some people with very oily scalps or heavy styling product use find sulfate-free formulas do not cleanse thoroughly enough.

Even then, a middle path works well: sulfate-free for regular washing, with an occasional clarifying wash when buildup becomes noticeable.

What to expect in the first two weeks

Switching is not always instantly pleasant, and this is where most people give up too early.

  • Less lather. Sulfate-free surfactants foam less. Lather has never been an indicator of cleaning power, but it feels like one. You may need two shorter washes instead of one.
  • A greasier feel for one to two weeks. Your scalp has been over-producing oil to compensate for aggressive cleansing. It takes a little time to recalibrate. This is temporary.
  • Softer texture within two to three washes. Usually the first thing people notice.
  • Color holding noticeably longer. Most obvious around week three or four, when you would normally start seeing fade.

Give it a full three weeks before judging.

Also check for sodium chloride

Plenty of shampoos marketed as sulfate-free still contain sodium chloride, ordinary salt, used to thicken the formula. It draws moisture out of hair and is particularly bad for keratin-treated hair. If it appears high in the ingredients list, the sulfate-free label is doing less for you than it suggests.

How to choose the right one

Sulfate-free is a baseline, not a complete specification. What matters next is what the formula adds back. These Evoque lines use sulfate-free cleansers:

  • Dry, brittle, color-treated hair: milk proteins and amino acids, Milk Therapy milk protein shampoo and conditioner.
  • Damaged, frizzy, chemically-treated hair: keratin and argan oil, Smart Keratin.
  • Frizz and humidity: sealing formulas, Miracle Touch.
  • Hair fall and dandruff: piroctone olamine and tea tree, Scalp Recovery.

Some specialist shampoos, such as purifying, deep-cleansing and purple toning formulas, do use sulfates because they are designed to remove buildup or deposit pigment. Always check the ingredient list on the product page; it is printed in full for every Evoque product in the shampoo range.

The short version

Sulfates are not dangerous. They are simply too harsh for hair that has been colored, bleached, keratin-treated or damaged, which describes most people reading this. If that is you, switching is one of the few hair care changes with a visible payoff, and the main thing it buys you is time: more weeks before your color fades, more months before your treatment gives out.

articles.title: How Often Should You Use Purple Shampoo? A Guide for Blonde, Silver and Platinum Hair
articles.excerpt: Once a week for most blondes, 1 to 2 times a week for platinum and bleached hair. A shade-by-shade guide, how long to leave it on, and how to fix over-toning.
articles.html:
Quick answer: most blondes should use purple shampoo once a week. Platinum, silver and heavily bleached hair can go to 1 to 2 times a week. Golden and honey blonde: every 1 to 2 weeks. Leave it on for 1 to 3 minutes, never more than 5, and always follow with conditioner or a mask.

Your hair How often Leave on
Platinum, silver, white 1 to 2 times a week 1 to 3 min
Bleached, high porosity 1 to 2 times a week, short contact 30 to 60 sec
Cool or ash blonde Once a week 1 to 2 min
Golden or honey blonde Every 1 to 2 weeks 1 min
Balayage, highlights Every 1 to 2 weeks, lightened sections only 1 to 2 min

Updated October 2026 by the Evoque Professional education team.

Purple shampoo is the most misused product in blonde hair care. Half of people don't use it often enough and complain their blonde looks orange within three weeks. The other half use it every wash and end up with a grey-lilac cast they then have to strip out.

The right answer depends on your shade, your porosity and what you are actually trying to fix.

Why purple works at all

It comes down to the color wheel. Purple sits directly opposite yellow. When you deposit a small amount of violet pigment onto hair showing yellow or brassy tones, the two cancel each other visually and the result reads as cleaner, cooler, more neutral blonde.

That is all purple shampoo does. It is a toner, not a treatment. It deposits pigment on the surface of the hair — it does not lighten, it does not repair, and it does not remove existing brass at a structural level. It masks warmth with its opposite.

Where the brass comes from

Understanding the cause helps you pick the right frequency:

  • Oxidation. Bleached hair is porous, and exposure to air, UV and heat gradually reveals underlying warm pigment.
  • Hard water. Minerals, especially iron, deposit on porous hair and turn it orange. If your blonde goes brassy unusually fast, water is often the culprit.
  • Chlorine and salt water. Both accelerate the process.
  • Heat styling. High temperatures push warmth out of the hair.
  • Product buildup. Yellowing from styling products, especially on white and silver hair.

How often: by shade

Platinum, white and silver hair

These shades show yellow fastest and need the most frequent toning. Use purple shampoo every second or third wash, roughly one to two times a week. If your hair is very porous, you may need it more often but with shorter contact time — 30 to 60 seconds rather than three minutes.

Cool and ash blonde

Once a week is usually right. This is the sweet spot for most blondes: enough to keep warmth suppressed, not enough to build up a visible violet cast.

Golden, honey and warm blonde

Every one to two weeks at most. Your blonde is meant to be warm. Over-toning here will make the color look flat, muddy and dull rather than cool. Use it as a correction when brass tips over into orange, not as routine maintenance.

Balayage, highlights and lived-in blonde

Every one to two weeks, applied only to the lightened sections. Do not pull purple shampoo through your natural root colour — you will create an unnatural contrast between the toned lengths and the untouched base.

Grey and white natural hair

Once or twice a week to counteract the yellowing that comes from environmental buildup and smoking, rather than from bleach.

Contact time matters more than frequency

This is the part most guides skip. Two minutes of purple shampoo once a week and thirty seconds three times a week deposit very different amounts of pigment.

Start conservatively: apply to wet hair, leave for one minute, rinse, and see the result when dry. If it is not cool enough, extend to two or three minutes next time. Never leave it longer than five minutes, and never sleep in it.

Porosity is the variable. Very damaged, high-porosity hair grabs pigment fast and can over-tone in 60 seconds. Healthy, low-porosity hair may need three or four minutes to shift anything at all.

Mask, mousse or shampoo?

Purple shampoo is not the only format, and often not the best one.

  • Purple shampoo gives the strongest, fastest correction. Best for regular maintenance on platinum and cool blonde. Shop the 1L salon size.
  • Purple mask tones and conditions at the same time. Bleached hair is dry hair, and a toning mask addresses both problems in one step. Best used weekly in place of your usual mask.
  • Purple mousse or toning foam is the gentlest and hardest to overdo. Because it is a leave-in, it tones gradually over days rather than all at once. Ideal if you have over-toned before, or if you have warm blonde and want subtle control. Try the Flawless Blonde Purple Toning Foam.

What to do if you have over-toned

Purple cast is temporary and fixable. It sits on the surface of the hair and will fade with washing.

  1. Stop using purple products immediately.
  2. Wash with a clarifying shampoo once or twice. This lifts surface deposit faster than a regular wash.
  3. Follow immediately with a deep treatment mask — clarifying is drying, and your hair is already porous.
  4. Wait. Most lilac casts clear within two to four washes.

Do not use bleach or color remover to correct over-toning. You will do far more damage than the problem warrants.

Five things that make purple shampoo work better

  • Apply to wet, not soaking, hair. Excess water dilutes the pigment before it can deposit.
  • Distribute evenly. Patchy application means patchy toning. Emulsify in your hands first.
  • Focus where the brass is. Usually mid-lengths and ends, not roots.
  • Wear gloves if you tone frequently — the pigment stains skin and nails.
  • Follow with conditioner or a mask every time. Toning shampoos are not moisturizing.

Frequently asked questions

How often should I use purple shampoo?

Once a week suits most blondes. Go up to one or two times a week for platinum and silver hair, and down to every one to two weeks for golden and warm shades.

How often should I use purple shampoo on blonde hair?

Once a week for most blonde hair, leaving it on for one to two minutes. Platinum, silver and bleached blonde can use it one to two times a week with short contact time, and golden blonde only every one to two weeks.

How often should you use purple shampoo on bleached hair?

One to two times a week, with short contact time. Bleached hair is porous and grabs violet pigment fast, so 30 to 60 seconds is often enough. Leave it longer only if your hair still looks yellow once it is fully dry.

Can you use purple shampoo every day?

Not recommended. Daily use builds up pigment and can leave a grey or lilac cast, and most toning shampoos are not moisturizing. Alternate with a gentle shampoo and use purple on one or two wash days a week.

How long should you leave purple shampoo on?

Start with one minute. Increase to two or three minutes if the result is not cool enough. Do not go past five minutes.

Should I use purple shampoo on wet or dry hair?

On wet hair that has been gently squeezed out. Dripping-wet hair dilutes the pigment; dry application deposits unevenly and is hard to control.

Does purple shampoo work on brown or brunette hair?

Only on lightened sections. Purple cancels yellow; brunette hair that turns orange needs blue toning instead.

Purple shampoo, mask or foam: which one should I use?

Shampoo gives the fastest correction. A purple mask tones and hydrates in one step, which suits dry bleached hair. A toning foam is the gentlest and the hardest to overdo. See the full Flawless Blonde range.

The bottom line

Once a week suits most blondes. Go up to two or three times a week for platinum and silver, down to every other week for golden and warm shades. Adjust based on what you see when your hair is dry, not wet — wet hair always looks cooler than it will when it dries.

And treat the underlying cause too. If hard water is turning your blonde orange every three weeks, a shower filter will do more for your color than any amount of purple shampoo.

A professional keratin treatment costs anywhere from $150 to $400 and should hold for three to five months. In practice, plenty of people find the smoothness gone in six or seven weeks and assume the treatment was poorly done. Usually it wasn't. The treatment failed at home, in the shower, within the first fortnight.

Here is what actually determines how long your results last.

The first 72 hours decide everything

Keratin treatments work by depositing keratin protein into the hair and sealing it in place with heat from a flat iron. That seal needs time to fully set. For the first 72 hours after your appointment:

  • Do not wash your hair. Water reopens the cuticle before the bond has stabilized.
  • Do not tie it up, clip it back or tuck it behind your ears. Any crease you set in the first three days can become permanent for the life of the treatment.
  • Do not wear a headband, hat or sunglasses pushed up on your head. Same reason.
  • Avoid sweating heavily. Salt in sweat behaves the same way as salt in seawater.

If your stylist told you 48 hours instead of 72, follow their instruction — formulas differ. But when in doubt, wait longer.

Sulfates are the single biggest cause of premature fade

This is the part most people get wrong. Sodium lauryl sulfate and sodium laureth sulfate are aggressive cleansing agents found in the majority of drugstore shampoos. They are extremely effective at removing oil — and equally effective at stripping the keratin you just paid for out of the hair shaft.

A single wash with a sulfate shampoo will not undo the treatment. Washing three times a week for a month absolutely will. Studies of keratin retention consistently show sulfate-containing cleansers accelerating protein loss compared to sulfate-free alternatives.

Switch to a sulfate-free keratin shampoo before your appointment, not after. The Smart Keratin Restorative Shampoo is formulated specifically to top up keratin with each wash rather than deplete it, using hydrolyzed keratin and amino acids alongside argan and macadamia oil.

Sulfate-free vs. gentle sulfate shampoos: what's the difference for keratin-treated hair?

A common debate in keratin aftercare communities is whether any sulfate is off-limits or whether mild sulfate formulations are acceptable. Here is a balanced look at both sides, so you can make an informed choice for your hair type and lifestyle.

Sulfate-free shampoos Gentle (mild) sulfate shampoos
Cleansing agents Amino acid or glucoside surfactants (e.g. sodium cocoyl glutamate, coco-glucoside) Low-concentration sodium laureth sulfate or sodium coco-sulfate
Lather Light to moderate — may feel different if you're used to traditional shampoos Richer lather, closer to conventional shampoos
Scalp buildup removal Effective for most scalp types; may need more product for very oily hair Stronger at cutting through heavy oil or product buildup
Potential effect on keratin Generally considered lower-risk for keratin retention, though individual results vary Milder than classic SLS formulas, but some research suggests even gentle sulfates may accelerate protein loss over time with frequent use
Salt content Varies — always check for sodium chloride in the first half of the ingredients list Varies — same caution applies
Best suited for Fine to medium hair; those prioritising treatment longevity; colour-treated hair Very thick, coarse, or oily hair that finds sulfate-free formulas insufficient

The honest answer is that the research on keratin longevity is not exhaustive, and everyone's hair responds differently. What is well-established is that high-concentration sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) — the harshest common surfactant — poses the greatest risk. Milder alternatives sit on a spectrum. If you have oily or very thick hair and a gentle sulfate formula is the only shampoo that leaves your scalp feeling clean, it may be a reasonable compromise. If your priority is maximum treatment life, a properly formulated sulfate-free option is the safer bet.

The Smart Keratin Restorative Shampoo is sulfate-free and formulated with hydrolyzed keratin and amino acids, designed to cleanse without depleting the treatment — a good starting point if you want to see how sulfate-free washing works for your hair type. Pair it with the Smart Keratin Restorative Conditioner to maintain moisture balance after every wash.

Also avoid sodium chloride

Check your shampoo label for sodium chloride — ordinary salt, used as a thickening agent. It is common even in some products marketed as sulfate-free, and it draws moisture and keratin out of treated hair. If it appears in the first half of the ingredients list, replace the product.

Wash less often, and wash cooler

Every wash costs you a small amount of treatment. Reducing frequency from daily to every second or third day can extend results by weeks. Keratin-treated hair typically gets less greasy anyway, because the smoother cuticle distributes scalp oil more evenly down the shaft.

Use lukewarm water rather than hot. Hot water lifts the cuticle and speeds protein loss. A cool final rinse helps seal it back down and adds visible shine.

Condition every single time

Skipping conditioner on keratin-treated hair is a mistake. The treatment leaves hair smoother but not necessarily more hydrated, and dry hair breaks. Use a matching keratin conditioner on mid-lengths and ends after every wash.

Once a week, replace it with a Smart Keratin Deep Treatment Mask. Five to ten minutes of contact time drives keratin and amino acids deeper into the cortex than a rinse-out conditioner can reach, effectively topping up the treatment between salon visits.

Protect against chlorine and salt water

Chlorine and seawater are both harsh on treated hair. If you swim regularly:

  • Wet your hair with clean water before getting in. Saturated hair absorbs less pool water.
  • Apply a leave-in conditioner or a light layer of hair oil as a barrier.
  • Rinse thoroughly immediately after swimming.
  • Wear a swim cap for regular lap swimming.

Heat styling: less, but not none

One of the points of a keratin treatment is that you need less heat styling — hair dries smoother on its own. Use that. When you do use a dryer or iron, always apply heat protection first. The Smart Keratin Frizz Control cream and leave-in sprays in the range protect up to 230°C.

Be careful with color timing

Do not color your hair in the two weeks after a keratin treatment. The sealed cuticle resists pigment, so color takes unevenly and the developer can compromise the treatment. If you want both, color first, then keratin — ideally at the same appointment or within a few days, with the keratin last.

A realistic weekly routine

  1. Wash days (2–3 per week): sulfate-free keratin shampoo, lukewarm water, cool final rinse.
  2. Every wash: keratin conditioner on mid-lengths and ends, two minutes minimum.
  3. Once weekly: deep treatment mask instead of conditioner, 5–10 minutes.
  4. Daily: a few drops of keratin argan oil on dry ends for shine and sealing.
  5. Before heat: always a heat protectant leave-in.

How long should it actually last?

With this routine, expect three to five months from a full keratin treatment, with the smoothness fading gradually rather than disappearing suddenly. Fine hair often holds it slightly longer than coarse hair. Very damaged or heavily bleached hair tends to release it faster, because the porous structure does not hold the protein as well — in that case, a bond-repair product like the Plex Extreme S.O.S line alongside your keratin aftercare will help.

The pattern is consistent: people who switch to sulfate-free care see months of results, and people who go back to their old shampoo see weeks.
